body: Slovakian bollards have orange double reflectors on the front and a white one on the back, with rare blue and red variants. This design is shared only with Czechia.
Slovakia and Czechia share a unique, wider type B guardrail. While Czechia uses it consistently, Slovakia sometimes uses other types.
Both Slovakia and Czechia commonly use wide, round concrete poles, often seen in pairs.
Poletops in Slovakia and Czechia typically feature short metal bars holding the insulators.
Poletops with two support bars forming an inverted triangle can be found in Slovakia and Czechia, but also in Germany, Albania, Serbia, and Romania.
Unique to Slovakia and Czechia are concrete poles with trident poletops, which have two arms angled upwards.
Both countries commonly have lamp posts with a thick base mounted by opposing pairs of bolts.
Temporary square signposts with red and white stripes are common in both Slovakia and Czechia.
Chevrons in Slovakia and Czechia are typically white with red arrows, with a less common red on yellow variant.
Striped gas and water poles can be found next to roads, but similar poles exist elsewhere in Europe.
Hiking markers with a colored stripe between two white ones are common in Slovakia and Czechia, but also seen in Poland, Hungary, and Germany.
Prefabricated apartment blocks are common, but in Slovakia and Czechia, they are often well-maintained with vibrant colours and patterns.
Roofs with diamond-shaped tiles are common in Slovakia and Czechia, and also seen in Hungary.
Much of the Generation 3 coverage features a car antenna with a grey piece of tape on top, a meta also found in Hungary, Romania, and Bulgaria.
In Generation 4 coverage, look for black signs displaying the road number at the end of bridges.

The Slovak language is distinct for its use of the letters Ĺ, Ô, Ä, Ŕ, and Ľ, while Czech uses Ř, Ě, and Ů. Both share acute accents on vowels (á, é, etc.), which distinguishes them from South Slavic languages.
Slovakia's landscape ranges from very mountainous to completely flat, while Czechia is generally hillier but less mountainous.
Slovak directional signs are blue with small white arrows, distinguishing them from the large filled-in arrows on Czech signs.
Slovak road signs often have the border painted right at the edge, unlike Czech signs where there is a gap.
Slovak highway signs, blue or green, have a border right at the edge, while Czech highway signs have a separated border.
The most common Slovak street signs are white with blue text and a thin red border. Czechia has similar signs but never uses the word 'ulica'.
Slovak house numbers are usually on white signs with a thin red or black border.
Slovak signposts usually have an open top, a grey metal cap, or a thin black cap, unlike the thick black caps common in Czechia.
Slovakia's pedestrian signs have five stripes, one featuring a person with a belt (like Germany) and another with condensed stripes.
Slovak road signs are characterized by a very bold font, which is much thinner on Czech signs.
Slovak kilometre markers are divided into two sections by a black horizontal line, a feature absent on Czech markers.
Unique to Slovakia, cycling signs use the letter 'C' as a symbol and often appear on a yellow post.
Window shutters are more common in Slovakia and Hungary than in Czechia.
Many Slovak and Hungarian houses have their short side facing the road with a hip end roof, a style less common in Czechia.
Grey metal roofs are very common in Slovakia, especially in the east, but less so in Czechia.
Slovakia has a lot of Generation 3 spring coverage, in contrast to the winter coverage often seen in Czechia.
The Slovak railway crossing sign is distinguished by its white rectangular background, which is absent on Czech signs.
Small signs with double signposts are a common sight in Slovakia, but rare for small signs in Czechia.
Slovakia has a new, rare bollard design similar to Hungary's: a wedge-shaped bollard with a red front reflector.
Wooden poles and white concrete supports are slightly more common in Slovakia than in Czechia.
Slovak phone numbers are 10 digits and include a 2-3 digit area code, unlike Czech numbers which generally don't start with 0.
Slovak road numbers for 3-digit (500-560) and 4-digit roads generally increase from west to east.
The tallest mountains are in central and northern Slovakia, while the flattest areas are in the southwest and southeast.
The western lowlands of Slovakia are characterized by completely flat agricultural fields that stretch to the horizon.
The eastern lowlands feature wide, flat fields with distant hills or mountains on the horizon.
Southern Slovakia has a large Hungarian population, so look for bilingual signs.
Concrete poles in the Nitra and Trnava regions often have yellow circles painted on them.
Yellow lamp posts with a blue base are a good indicator for eastern Slovakia and the city of Zvolen.
Northern Slovakia has two wide valleys surrounded by tall mountains, distinguishable by the direction of the closest mountains.
Pine forests are common in the far western part of Slovakia.
In the northeast Prešov region, look for bilingual town signs in Rusyn, a Cyrillic-based language.
Bratislava is the largest city and the only major one with a large river running through it.
Bratislava (red) and Košice (yellow-blue-white) are the only cities with trams, and their buses share these color schemes.
Trolleybuses can be found in Bratislava, Košice, Prešov, Žilina and Banská Bystrica. Each city has its own distinct livery.
Skalica in the northwest has red street signs similar to Czechia, but with a distinctive stylized font.
Čičmany in the western Žilina Region is known for dark brown wooden houses decorated with white line art.
